t: The CPU and the fetch–execute cycle
l: Hello and welcome to Digital Tech Revision, the podcast for CCEA GCSE Digital Technology. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is lesson L13: The CPU and the fetch to execute cycle.
So Conor, if someone only remembers one thing from today, what should it be?
Explain the purpose of the CPU using processing language, not just 'the brain'. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

The central processing unit (CPU) is the part of a computer that does the processing. It is a microprocessor, which means all of its circuits are built onto a single chip. Its purpose is to process data and carry out the instructions that make up computer programs. Every program, from a game on your phone to the till software in a shop in Belfast, is really a long list of simple instructions held in memory.
Makes sense. Keep going.

The CPU works through these instructions one after another by repeatedly fetching an instruction from memory, decoding it to find out what it means, and then executing it. This repeating process is called the fetch to execute cycle. While doing this, the CPU also manages the rest of the computer by sending control signals to memory and to input and output devices. People often call the CPU the brain of the computer, but in an exam you must explain what it actually does: it processes data and executes program instructions.
Right. What else do we need to know?

The CPU has three main components. The control unit manages the running of instructions. It decides which instruction is next, fetches it, decodes it and then sends control signals to the other parts so that the instruction is carried out. It co-ordinates everything but does not do the calculations itself. The arithmetic logic unit (ALU) does the calculations and the logic. Arithmetic means adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing.
Got it. Keep going.

Logic means comparisons and the operators AND, OR and NOT, which let a program make decisions, such as checking whether a pupil has enough money on their canteen card. The ALU contains a special register called the accumulator, which holds the result of each calculation until it is stored back in memory. The immediate-access store (IAS) is the main memory. It holds the programs and data currently in use. Each memory location has a unique address, so the CPU can go straight to the instruction or data it needs.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

A register is a very small, very fast memory location inside the CPU, used for one particular job. Five matter at GCSE. The program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched. Because most instructions run in order, it goes up by one after each fetch. The memory address register (MAR) holds the address of the memory location that is about to be read from or written to.
Okay. Keep going.

The memory data register (MDR) holds the actual instruction or data that has just been fetched from memory, or that is about to be written to memory; all data going between the CPU and main memory passes through it. The instruction address register (IAR), as CCEA describes it, holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed; some textbooks call this the instruction register. Finally, the accumulator in the ALU holds the result of the latest calculation. A quick way to remember the difference: the MAR holds where, the MDR holds what.
Go on.

In the fetch stage, the address held in the program counter is copied into the MAR. The control unit then reads that memory location, and the instruction stored there is copied into the MDR and then into the IAR. The program counter is increased by one so that it points to the next instruction. In the decode stage, the control unit works out what the instruction means, for example whether it is asking for a value to be loaded, two numbers to be added or a result to be stored. In the execute stage, the instruction is carried out.
Right. Keep going.

If it needs data from memory, the data's address goes into the MAR and the data comes back through the MDR. If it needs a calculation or comparison, the ALU does it and the result goes into the accumulator. The cycle then starts again with the next address in the program counter. A modern CPU repeats this cycle billions of times every second.
Time for quickfire key terms. I'll say the term, and you give me the answer the mark scheme gives credit for.
Go for it.
CPU?
Central processing unit. A microprocessor whose purpose is to process data and carry out the instructions of programs, managing the functions of the computer.
ALU?
Arithmetic logic unit: the part of the CPU that carries out arithmetic calculations and logical operations and comparisons.
Control unit?
The part of the CPU that fetches and decodes instructions and sends control signals to co-ordinate the other components.
Immediate-access store?
Main memory (RAM) holding the programs and data currently in use; each location has a unique address.
Register?
A very small, very fast memory location inside the CPU used for a specific purpose.
Program counter?
Register holding the address of the next instruction to be fetched; incremented after each fetch.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

This topic comes up nearly every year. You have been asked to explain the purpose of the CPU, describe the ALU and control unit, explain registers and the cycle, and write a levelled answer on the ALU and immediate-access store. Marks are given for each correct role, so 'describe' means say what the part does, not just name it. For the CPU's purpose, say it processes data and carries out program instructions; 'it is the brain' scores nothing on its own. Write every acronym in full at least once, as examiners regularly report lost marks for this. In fetch to execute questions, give the steps in the right order and name the register used at each step. Common mistakes are saying the ALU decodes instructions, mixing up the MAR and the MDR, and forgetting that the program counter is incremented. In levelled questions, use correct technical terms and link each point to the cycle.

Let's finish with a question for the listeners. Which register holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched? Is it A, Program counter; B, Memory data register; C, Accumulator; D, Instruction address register?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is A: Program counter. The program counter holds the next address and is increased by one after each fetch.
